questions.question: Explain who a textile brief is written for and how that changes it, write the brief sentence for the shelter fabric and show how it traces back to the investigations, and convert the water and flame tests into specifications.
questions.expected_answer: The textile brief is written for a supplier or factory who will not see the team's tests and must be told exactly what to supply, and for an inspector who must check the delivered fabric against the words, so every line must be checkable. The brief: a waterproof, flame-retardant, lightweight, hard-wearing fabric for the roof and walls of a family emergency shelter covering 21 square metres, to be erected by displaced families in South African rain, wind, sun and cold and to protect them for at least a month while cooking and heating with paraffin or gas take place inside. Waterproof and flame-retardant trace to the textile tests, lightweight to the transport requirement, hard-wearing to the month and the wind, South African conditions to the scenarios and cooking inside to the health and safety list. Waterproofing: no penetration in the five-minute drip test of 50 millilitres from 100 millimetres and a dry towel under the ten-second thumb pressure test, with the industry equivalent of a hydrostatic head of at least 1 500 millimetres. Flame: after three seconds in a candle flame it must not sustain a flame, must not melt or drip, must self-extinguish within two seconds, charring allowed, with certification to a recognised flame-retardant standard for tent fabrics.

questions.question: List the ten specifications for the shelter textile with the number or test behind each, and the constraints that belong in the second column.
questions.expected_answer: One, waterproofing: no penetration in the drip test and dry under thumb pressure, hydrostatic head at least 1 500 millimetres. Two, flame: no sustained flame, no melting or dripping, self-extinguishing within two seconds, recognised standard. Three, mass: at most 350 grams per square metre so a 30 square metre cover is under 11 kilograms and the bundle can be carried by two people. Four, strength: a 20 millimetre cut must not tear further when pulled by hand, abrasion resistance at frame contacts, ripstop weave preferred. Five, UV resistance: strength and waterproofing retained after a month of sun through a UV-stabilised fibre or coating. Six, opacity and colour: opaque when lit from inside, light roof colour to reflect sun, stated colour visible from the air. Seven, breathability: non-breathing permitted only with the shelter's specified ventilation openings. Eight, seams: heat-welded or taped, no plain sewn seams, drip-tested on a seam sample. Nine, fixings: eyelets or webbing loops at 500 millimetre spacing, reinforced with a second layer, without tearing. Ten, handling: folds without cracking at minus 5 degrees and does not stick to itself at 40 degrees. Constraints: cost per square metre from a price list, about R60 to R90, so a cover is under R3 000; produced or stocked in South Africa and deliverable within two weeks in quantities of a thousand; eyelet spacing compatible with the frame design; recyclable or reusable where possible. Lines about the fabric are specifications; lines about the programme are constraints.

questions.question: Show how the tested samples are eliminated against the specification, state the recommended textiles and the honest compromise, and describe how the page is laid out and checked.
questions.expected_answer: Untreated canvas fails waterproofing and flame; waxed canvas fails the pressure test and flame and is heavy; silicone-treated canvas fails pressure and wear; plain polypropylene tarpaulin passes water, mass and cost but fails flame badly and UV; truck-grade PVC-coated polyester passes water, ignition and strength but fails mass and raises toxic smoke; flame-retardant-treated, acrylic- or polyurethane-coated, UV-stabilised ripstop polyester or light canvas at about 300 grams per square metre passes every line at a higher price. The recommendation is that fabric for roof and walls with a heavier, cheaper coated tarpaulin for the groundsheet where pressure resistance matters more than flame. The compromise is stated honestly: the chosen fabric costs about twice the tarpaulin, a fixed budget might choose tarpaulin and manage fire by spacing, outdoor cooking and lamps, and the brief says which is recommended for which scenario and why, and lists what the classroom could not test, hydrostatic head, tear strength in newtons, the flame standard and UV ageing, for supplier certification. The page has the brief sentence at the top, numbered specifications with test and number in one column, constraints in a second, the justified recommendation, the further tests, with results tables and a labelled sample attached; a team mate reads it as the supplier to see if they can quote and as the inspector to see if every line can be tested.
